notes:
These notes on Haggai 1 come from the commentaries I was able to open, including Guzik, the older writers collected on BibleHub and StudyLight, Utley on bible.org, TGC (Barrett) and the Catholic Encyclopedia. The Enduring Word and TGC pages came back cut off partway through, so some of their verse notes are missing.

**v. 1**
- **The date.** Guzik dates the start of the prophecy to September 520 B.C. He says this makes Haggai the first of the three prophets who spoke after the exile. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/haggai-1/)
- **A pagan king's calendar.** The date is counted by a pagan king's reign because Israel had no king. Guzik quotes Spurgeon: God keeps count of the days His people delay in obeying. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/haggai-1/)
- **A feast day.** Utley notes that the message came on a new-moon festival day. (https://bible.org/seriespage/haggai-1-0)
- **The leaders.** Utley says Zerubbabel means "born in Babylon" and that he was of David's line. Joshua was grandson of the high priest killed in 586 B.C., and his name is the Hebrew form of "Jesus." (https://bible.org/seriespage/haggai-1-0)
- **Haggai's name.** Guzik says it probably means "festival of Yahweh." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/haggai-1/)

**v. 2**
- **A spiritual-sounding excuse.** The people didn't argue against building the temple. They argued about timing, claiming it wasn't God's time yet. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/haggai-1/)
- **Possible reasons.** Guzik suggests they may have thought Jeremiah's 70 years weren't finished yet, and he calls this unbelief. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/haggai-1/)
- **"This people."** Guzik notes God says "this people," not "My people." Utley says the phrase is used in a negative sense elsewhere in Isaiah. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/haggai-1/; https://bible.org/seriespage/haggai-1-0)

**vv. 3–4**
- **Wrong priorities.** Guzik says the problem wasn't nice houses in themselves. It was living in comfort while God's house lay in ruins. He quotes Trapp: Solomon built God's house first and his own second. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/haggai-1/)
- **"Paneled."** Utley says the word usually refers to covering walls with costly material, which suggests luxury. (https://bible.org/seriespage/haggai-1-0)

**v. 5**
- **"Set your heart on your ways."** That is the literal sense of "consider your ways." Calvin says it means thinking about one's conduct seriously, not just glancing at it. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/haggai/1-5.html)
- **What to consider.** Jerome, cited by Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB), says to look at both what they had done and what they had suffered. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haggai/1-5.htm)
- **A repeated call.** The Cambridge Bible notes Haggai uses the phrase four times in the book. (same URL)
- **Mind, feelings and will.** Barrett (TGC) says the Hebrew phrase covers all three. (https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/haggai/)

**v. 6**
- **A double curse.** Guzik: they harvested little, and even that little drained away. He links this to the warnings God gave through Moses. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/haggai-1/)
- **Two kinds of loss.** Barnes sees poor harvests, and also bodies that food and clothing failed to satisfy or warm. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haggai/1-6.htm)
- **The "bag with holes."** JFB calls it a proverb for wasted labour and money. He contrasts it with the heavenly purses that never wear out (Luke 12:33). (same URL)
- **Past, not future.** Calvin says the verbs describe what was already happening, not a coming punishment. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/haggai-1.html)

**v. 7**
- **Calvin on the repeated call.** The second "consider" aims to turn their sloth into hard work, not just to make them hate sin. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/haggai-1.html)
- **Kelly.** The first call rebukes; the second encourages and urges. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/haggai/1-3.html)

**v. 8**
- **Three commands.** Utley lists them: go up, bring wood, build. He thinks the hills were probably local forest, not Lebanon, since hauling timber that far would cost too much. (https://bible.org/seriespage/haggai-1-0)
- **God wants our part.** Guzik uses William Carey's story to argue that God chooses to work through people. He adds that the work must aim to please and glorify God. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/haggai-1/)

**v. 9**
- **"Why?"** Calvin says God asks not because He doesn't know, but to shake them awake. His hand doesn't strike blindly. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/haggai-1.html)
- **"Blew away."** Utley says the problems were not normal farming cycles but God's displeasure. (https://bible.org/seriespage/haggai-1-0)

**vv. 10–11**
- **Nature under God's control.** Utley ties the drought to the blessings and curses of the covenant (Deuteronomy 27–28). He notes that grain, wine and oil were the land's staple goods. (https://bible.org/seriespage/haggai-1-0)
- **Misreading the drought.** Guzik suggests the people may have blamed the drought on Satan and prayed against it. The page cut off before he finished this point. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/haggai-1/)

**v. 12**
- **They took it as God's word.** Matthew Henry says the people received the message as God's word, not man's. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/haggai/1-13.html)
- **Fear leads to service.** Henry: "if we fear him not, we shall not serve him." (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/haggai/1-14.html)
- **The leaders led the way.** Barrett notes the civil and religious leaders led the people's response. (https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/haggai/)
- **"Feared."** The NET Bible translates it "began to respect the Lord." (https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=hag+1:12-15)

**v. 13**
- **God responds at once.** JFB says that as soon as the people were willing to obey, even before work began, God's tone turned tender. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haggai/1-13.htm)
- **"The LORD's messenger."** The Pulpit Commentary says Haggai alone among the prophets uses this title for himself. (same URL)
- **A messenger, not an angel.** The same word can mean "angel." Keil says it means messenger here, and that many in the church fathers' time misread it. (same URL)
- **"I am with you."** In Hebrew it is just "I with you." Barnes says all of a creature's needs are summed up in those words. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/haggai/1-13.html)
- **Calvin.** We only obey from the heart when we lean on God's promises. (same URL)
- **Clarke (Methodist).** He compares Haggai's title to the "angels" of the seven churches in Revelation. (same URL)

**v. 14**
- **God stirs them.** Keil: to stir someone's spirit means to make them willing and glad to act. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haggai/1-14.htm)
- **Revival is God's work.** JFB: every revival of faith comes directly from God's Spirit. (same URL)
- **Leaders and people.** Guzik notes the stirring began with the leaders and spread to the people. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/haggai-1/)

**Where traditions differ (v. 14)**
- **Reformed: God moves first.**
  - The Geneva Bible note says people can't obey until God changes their hearts (John 6:44). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haggai/1-14.htm)
  - A comment collected in the Biblical Illustrator argues against the view that Israel obeyed first by free will and the Spirit then helped. It says God stirred them, and that is why they listened. (https://biblehub.com/sermons/haggai/1-14.htm)
- **Methodist: Clarke.** He stresses that the Spirit must strengthen the soul, not just inform the mind, before good work can be done. He doesn't take up the question of who moves first. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/haggai/1-14.html)

**v. 15**
- **About three weeks later.** Keil: the work began 23 days after Haggai's first message. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haggai/1-14.htm)
- **Gathering, not yet building.** JFB thinks they were gathering materials at this stage. He cites Grotius that the foundations weren't laid until three months later (2:18). (same URL)

**Catholic views**
- **Main message.** The Catholic Encyclopedia says Haggai urged the people to resume building and not be distracted by their luxurious homes. It also says he treated the drought as punishment for their neglect. (https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/01209d.htm)
- **Meaning of the temple.** It calls the temple "that outward symbol of the Divine presence among them". (same URL)
- **Haggai as an angel? (v. 13)** It rejects the Jewish tradition that Haggai was an angel in human form. (https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/aggeus) The Pulpit Commentary says the Greek Old Testament's wording started this idea, and Jerome refuted it. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haggai/1-13.htm)

**Not found**
- Any Orthodox (oca.org), Lutheran, Pentecostal or Anglican reading specific to this chapter.
- Bible Odyssey material.
- Any source describing a prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace reading of verse 6.
